children: A federal judge has blocked President Trump's name from immediately going back on the front of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, the latest twist in the continuing legal saga over the president's attempts to overhaul the cultural institution in the nation's capital.

Judge Christopher Cooper in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday denied the latest attempt by the venue's board to affix an inscription that says "renovated and restored by Donald J. Trump" under President John F. Kennedy's name on the front portico and prohibited it from renaming the grounds of the center after Trump.

Cooper said the renaming violates the order he issued in May, which required Trump's name to be removed from the building-where the board, stacked with the president's appointees, had voted to add it. Only Congress has the authority to rename the institution, he ruled at the time.

While Cooper said in Tuesday's decision that he appreciated how major supporters of cultural institutions are routinely recognized with prominent inscriptions on buildings and in other public areas, "Congress had other ideas for the Kennedy Center."
"It limited such memorials and donor recognitions to discrete (and discreet) areas, so as not to detract from the Center's function as an ongoing memorial to President Kennedy," he said.

Cooper, an Obama appointee, said he wouldn't decide now if the board can lawfully add a second inscription in the future-which would say "endowed by The Trump Kennedy Center Fund"-because the board said that won't be added until the private endowment it created in June has raised $100 million.

"The Fund has raised nothing yet," Cooper said. He directed the board to notify him when the endowment has raised the money and give the court at least 60 day's notice before it installs an inscription.

The judge's decision comes ahead of a planned meeting in which the center's board is expected to vote on a new resolution to immediately close the center's main building for two years for renovations. Trump said in a social-media post earlier Tuesday that the building is in such bad shape that people could be hurt if it is kept open.
